# Writing your own functions {#sec-own-functions} Sooner or later every analysis needs a calculation that no package provides — an index from a paper, a data check specific to your field protocol, a summary your lab always reports. This chapter is about turning that calculation into a function that is easy to call, hard to misuse, documented and tested. @sec-functions introduced the syntax. Here the focus is on what makes a function good: sensible arguments, clear errors, a docstring, and tests that tell you when you break it. ::: {.callout-note} ## Where this chapter comes from This chapter and @sec-resampling are **inspired by** the programming and resampling modules of **ecoR** [@oliveira_ecor], the R course wiki of the Instituto de Biociências, Universidade de São Paulo, produced and maintained by Alexandre Adalardo de Oliveira. The idea of building ecological indices as functions, step by step, comes from there. The text, examples and exercises here are written from scratch for Julia; the authors of ecoR have not reviewed this book. If you read Portuguese and want to go further, the original material is freely available (CC BY-SA 4.0): - [9. Noções de Programação](https://ecor.ib.usp.br/doku.php?id=03_apostila:programar_ale) — the course notes on programming; - [9. Criando Funções Básicas](https://ecor.ib.usp.br/doku.php?id=02_tutoriais:tutorial8:start) — the step-by-step tutorial; - [exercises on functions](https://ecor.ib.usp.br/doku.php?id=01_curso_atual:exercicios9), automatically graded in [notaR](http://notar.ib.usp.br), in R. ::: ::: {#cell-setup-09 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using TidierData using DataFrames, CSV using Statistics using Test ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("..", "data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) nrow(ponds) ``` ::: {#setup-09 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 180 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Exercises in this chapter As in @sec-julia-basics, most answers here are functions you write, which `check` calls on its own test inputs. Start each session with: ```julia include("exercises/check.jl") using TidierData, DataFrames, CSV, Statistics, Test ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) ``` ::: ## From a calculation to a function {#sec-fn-calculation} Suppose you want to know how variable richness is across ponds, relative to its mean. The coefficient of variation answers that, and it is one line: ::: {#cell-cv-inline .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} std(ponds.richness) / mean(ponds.richness) * 100 ``` ::: {#cv-inline .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 68.12190985250986 ``` ::: ::: The moment you want it for a second variable, or per region, the line becomes a function. Give it a name that says what it computes, and the argument a name that says what it expects: ::: {#cell-cv-function .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} cv(x) = std(x) / mean(x) * 100 cv(ponds.richness), cv(ponds.body_size) ``` ::: {#cv-function .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (68.12190985250986, 9.971208205402203) ``` ::: ::: Richness varies far more, relative to its mean, than body size does. A function can return several things at once. The idiomatic way is a **named tuple**, whose fields you read by name: ::: {#cell-named-tuple .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} count_summary(x) = (n = length(x), mean = mean(x), var = var(x)) s = count_summary(ponds.richness) s.mean, s.var ``` ::: {#named-tuple .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (7.133333333333334, 23.613407821229057) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 10.1 — Variance-to-mean ratio For counts, the variance-to-mean ratio says how individuals — or species — are spread across sampling units. If the counts follow a Poisson distribution, variance equals the mean and the ratio is about 1; above 1 the counts are more clumped, below 1 more even. Write `vmr(x)` and check it with `check("10.1", vmr)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Same shape as `cv`: one line, `var` over `mean`. `var` is the sample variance, which divides by $n - 1$. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-10-1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} vmr(x) = var(x) / mean(x) vmr(ponds.richness) ``` ::: {#answer-10-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3.310290816060148 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-10-1-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("10.1", vmr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: Richness across all 180 ponds has a ratio of about 3.3: far more variable than a Poisson with a single mean. That does not yet mean the counting process is odd — the ponds differ in area, canopy and region. @sec-fn-groups returns to this. ::: ::: ## Arguments: defaults and keywords {#sec-fn-arguments} A function often has a sensible default that the user may want to change. `cv` returns a percentage; someone might prefer a proportion. There are two ways to offer that. A **positional argument with a default** comes after the others and is set by position: ::: {#cell-positional-default .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} cv_pos(x, percent = true) = std(x) / mean(x) * (percent ? 100 : 1) cv_pos(ponds.richness), cv_pos(ponds.richness, false) ``` ::: {#positional-default .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (68.12190985250986, 0.6812190985250985) ``` ::: ::: A **keyword argument** goes after a semicolon and is always set by name: ::: {#cell-keyword .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} cv_kw(x; percent = true) = std(x) / mean(x) * (percent ? 100 : 1) cv_kw(ponds.richness; percent = false) ``` ::: {#keyword .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.6812190985250985 ``` ::: ::: For options like this, keywords are the better choice: `cv_kw(x; percent = false)` says what it does, while `cv_pos(x, false)` makes the reader look up what `false` means. A function can also collect keywords it does not know and pass them on with `kwargs...`. Here `rounded_cv` handles `digits` itself and hands everything else to `cv_kw`: ::: {#cell-kwargs-forward .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} rounded_cv(x; digits = 1, kwargs...) = round(cv_kw(x; kwargs...); digits) rounded_cv(ponds.richness), rounded_cv(ponds.richness; percent = false, digits = 3) ``` ::: {#kwargs-forward .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (68.1, 0.681) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.r-equivalent} **In R** R has one kind of argument, which can be given by position or by name. Julia separates them: arguments before the `;` are positional, those after are keywords and must be named. `kwargs...` plays the role of R's `...` when forwarding options to another function. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 10.2 — Standardizing, with options Write `standardize(x; center = true, scale = true)`. By default it returns $(x - \bar x) / s$; `center = false` skips subtracting the mean and `scale = false` skips dividing by the standard deviation. Check it with `check("10.2", standardize)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Build the result in two steps, each depending on its option: `centered = center ? x .- mean(x) : x`, then divide `centered` by `std(x)` only if `scale` is true. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#answer-10-2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function standardize(x; center = true, scale = true) centered = center ? x .- mean(x) : x return scale ? centered ./ std(x) : centered end check("10.2", standardize) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: `std(x)` is computed on the original `x`, so it is the same whether or not you center. ::: ::: ## Refusing bad input {#sec-fn-errors} A function that quietly returns nonsense is worse than one that stops. `cv` has two blind spots: ::: {#cell-cv-nonsense .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} cv([0, 0, 0]), cv([-5, 5]) ``` ::: {#cv-nonsense .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (NaN, Inf) ``` ::: ::: `NaN` for an empty pond survey, and an infinite coefficient for data with a negative value, which counts cannot have. Checks at the top of the function catch both, and `throw(ArgumentError(...))` tells the caller that the problem is the input, not the function: ::: {#cell-cv-checked .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function cv_checked(x) any(<(0), x) && throw(ArgumentError("values must be non-negative")) mean(x) > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the CV is undefined")) return std(x) / mean(x) * 100 end try cv_checked([-5, 5]) catch e e end ``` ::: {#cv-checked .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ArgumentError("values must be non-negative") ``` ::: ::: The `condition && action` form reads as "if condition, then action"; `condition || action` as "unless condition, action". Both are idiomatic for checks like these. ::: {.callout-tip} ## `@assert` is for your own mistakes `@assert condition` stops when something that should never happen does. Use it to check your own reasoning inside a function; use `ArgumentError` for input that a user could plausibly get wrong. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 10.3 — A safer `vmr` Rewrite `vmr` so that it throws an `ArgumentError` when it gets fewer than two values, any negative value, or a mean of zero, and still returns the ratio otherwise. Check it with `check("10.3", vmr)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Three checks, one line each, before the calculation. `length(x) < 2`, `any(<(0), x)` and `mean(x) == 0` are the conditions. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#answer-10-3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function vmr(x) length(x) < 2 && throw(ArgumentError("need at least two values")) any(<(0), x) && throw(ArgumentError("counts cannot be negative")) mean(x) == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the ratio is undefined")) return var(x) / mean(x) end check("10.3", vmr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: This replaces the one-line `vmr` from 10.1: a method with the same argument types overwrites the old one. ::: ::: ## Documenting a function {#sec-fn-docs} A string placed immediately before a function becomes its **docstring**, which is what `?cv_documented` shows in the REPL and what VS Code shows when you hover over the name. The convention is the signature indented by four spaces, then one or two sentences on what the function does and returns: ::: {#cell-docstring .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} """ cv_documented(x; percent = true) Coefficient of variation of `x`: the standard deviation divided by the mean, times 100 unless `percent = false`. Throws an `ArgumentError` if the mean is zero. """ function cv_documented(x; percent = true) mean(x) > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the CV is undefined")) return std(x) / mean(x) * (percent ? 100 : 1) end ``` ::: {#docstring .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` Main.Notebook.cv_documented ``` ::: ::: ::: {.r-equivalent} **In R** Docstrings play the role of `roxygen2` comments, with one difference: they are part of the language, available as soon as the function is defined, with no build step. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 10.4 — Document `vmr` Add a docstring to your `vmr` from 10.3: the signature, what the ratio means, and which inputs it refuses. Run the definition again and try `?vmr` in the REPL. Then check it with `check("10.4", vmr)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint The docstring goes directly above `function vmr(x)`, with nothing in between — not even a blank line. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#answer-10-4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} """ vmr(x) Variance-to-mean ratio of the counts `x`. About 1 for Poisson counts, above 1 when counts are clumped, below 1 when they are more even. Throws an `ArgumentError` for fewer than two values, negative values, or a zero mean. """ function vmr(x) length(x) < 2 && throw(ArgumentError("need at least two values")) any(<(0), x) && throw(ArgumentError("counts cannot be negative")) mean(x) == 0 && throw(ArgumentError("the mean is zero; the ratio is undefined")) return var(x) / mean(x) end check("10.4", vmr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Your function, per group {#sec-fn-groups} A function you write works inside a Tidier pipeline — with one catch. Tidier knows that `mean`, `std` or `sum` summarize a whole column, but it does not know that about your `cv`. By default it applies unknown functions to **each value separately**, which here would compute a coefficient of variation for every single pond: ::: {#cell-cv-per-region-wrong .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} wrong = @chain ponds begin @group_by(region) @summarize(cv_richness = cv(richness)) end nrow(wrong), first(wrong.cv_richness, 3) ``` ::: {#cv-per-region-wrong .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (180, [NaN, NaN, NaN]) ``` ::: ::: 180 rows of `NaN` instead of three numbers, and no error. Putting `~` in front of the function tells Tidier to pass it the whole column: ::: {#cell-cv-per-region .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @chain ponds begin @group_by(region) @summarize(cv_richness = ~cv(richness), cv_body = ~cv(body_size)) end ``` ::: {#cv-per-region .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

3Cerrado60.81189.92402
``` ::: ::: The same with `DataFrames.jl` directly (@sec-native-dataframes), where the question does not arise: ::: {#cell-cv-per-region-native .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} combine(groupby(ponds, :region), :richness => cv => :cv_richness) ``` ::: {#cv-per-region-native .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Check the number of rows After `@summarize`, you should have one row per group. If you have one row per observation, Tidier has applied your function to each value: add the `~`. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 10.5 — Is richness clumped within regions? Compute the variance-to-mean ratio of `richness` for each region, in a column called `vmr`, using your function. Check it with `check("10.5", by_region)`. Are the ratios closer to 1 than the value for all ponds together? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint The `~cv` block of this section, with `~vmr` in place of `~cv`. Without the `~`, your `vmr` from 10.3 receives one pond at a time and rightly refuses it: "need at least two values". ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#answer-10-5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} by_region = @chain ponds begin @group_by(region) @summarize(vmr = ~vmr(richness)) end check("10.5", by_region) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: The ratios, from about 1.8 to 3.2, are all lower than for the pooled ponds (3.3): part of the variation came from differences between regions. They are still above 1, because ponds within a region differ in area and canopy. In @sec-overdispersion a Poisson model that accounts for these predictors had no overdispersion left. A ratio above 1 in raw counts is a reason to look for predictors, not proof that the counts are not Poisson. ::: ::: ## Functions that take functions {#sec-fn-higher-order} In Julia, functions are values: they can be stored in a vector, passed to another function, or written without a name. That makes it easy to apply several summaries at once: ::: {#cell-several-summaries .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} [f(ponds.richness) for f in (mean, median, cv, vmr)] ``` ::: {#several-summaries .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{Float64}: 7.133333333333334 6.0 68.12190985250986 3.310290816060148 ``` ::: ::: An **anonymous function** is written `x -> expression`. `map` applies one to every element of a collection — here, to three columns of the data: ::: {#cell-anonymous .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} map(col -> round(cv(col); digits = 1), eachcol(ponds[:, [:area_m2, :temp_c, :body_size]])) ``` ::: {#anonymous .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 117.6 11.6 10.0 ``` ::: ::: Area varies enormously between ponds, temperature very little: the coefficient of variation puts variables with different units on the same scale. ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 10.6 — Morisita's index Morisita's index of dispersion compares how often two individuals picked at random fall in the same sampling unit with what a random spread would give: $$ I_d = n \, \frac{\sum_i x_i (x_i - 1)}{N (N - 1)} $$ where $x_i$ is the count in unit $i$, $n$ the number of units and $N = \sum_i x_i$. It is about 1 for a random spread and above 1 for a clumped one. Write `morisita(x)`, check it with `check("10.6", morisita)`, and apply it to these counts of tadpole clusters in ten quadrats along a pond margin: ::: {#cell-data-10-6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} quadrats = [0, 3, 0, 0, 7, 1, 0, 0, 5, 0] ``` ::: {#data-10-6 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10-element Vector{Int64}: 0 3 0 0 7 1 0 0 5 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint `x .* (x .- 1)` gives $x_i(x_i - 1)$ for every unit at once; `sum` adds them up. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-10-6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function morisita(x) N = sum(x) return length(x) * sum(x .* (x .- 1)) / (N * (N - 1)) end morisita(quadrats) ``` ::: {#answer-10-6 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2.8333333333333335 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-10-6-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("10.6", morisita) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: About 2.8: the clusters are strongly clumped, in three of the ten quadrats. A version for real use would refuse `N < 2`, as in 10.3. ::: ::: ## Testing your functions {#sec-fn-tests} `check` has been testing your functions against inputs whose answers are known. You can do the same for your own functions with the `Test` standard library, and rerun the tests every time you change the code: ::: {#testset .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @testset "cv_checked" begin @test cv_checked([10, 10, 10]) == 0 # no variation @test cv_checked([1, 2, 3]) ≈ 50 # std 1, mean 2 @test_throws ArgumentError cv_checked([0, 0]) @test_throws ArgumentError cv_checked([-1, 1]) end; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Test Summary: | Pass  Total  Time
cv_checked    |    4      4  0.2s
``` ::: ::: ::: Good tests use cases you can work out by hand, and include the inputs the function should refuse. Type `≈` as `\approx` followed by `Tab`; it compares floating-point numbers with a tolerance, where `==` would fail over rounding. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Where your functions should live Once a function is useful beyond one script, move it to a file of its own — say `functions.jl` in your project folder — and load it with `include("functions.jl")` at the top of each analysis. The tests can live in a second file next to it. When the collection grows, the next step is a package, which `Pkg` can create for you with `Pkg.generate`. ::: ## Challenges {.unnumbered} 1. Write a `@testset` for your `morisita` with cases you can compute by hand: all individuals in one unit, and exactly one individual per unit. What should each give? 2. Add a `Matrix` method to `vmr` (@sec-dispatch) that returns one ratio per column, treating each column as a species counted across quadrats (rows). 3. `cv` fails on a column with missing values, such as `canopy`. Add a keyword `skipmissing = false` that, when true, ignores them. Which default is safer, and why?
